tasks.description: Use `re.search()` to check if the string 'Hello, World!' contains the word 'World'. Print True or False.
tasks.hint:
`import re` — then `re.search(pattern, string)` returns a match object if found, None if not.
`bool(re.search('World', 'Hello, World!'))` → `True`
Or check with `if re.search(...): print(True)`
tasks.walkthrough:
`search` finds the pattern anywhere in the string and returns a match object, which counts as True.
`bool()` turns that into a plain True for printing.

tasks.description: Use `re.findall()` to extract all numbers from the string 'I have 3 cats and 12 dogs and 1 fish'. Print the list.
tasks.hint:
`re.findall(pattern, string)` returns a list of ALL matches.
Pattern `r'\d+'` matches one or more digits (`\d` = any digit, `+` = one or more).
`re.findall(r'\d+', text)` → `['3', '12', '1']` (strings, not ints).
tasks.solution:
import re

text = 'I have 3 cats and 12 dogs and 1 fish'
print(re.findall(r'\d+', text))
tasks.walkthrough:
`\d` matches a digit and `+` means one or more in a row, so `12` is caught as a whole rather than as 1 and 2.
`findall` returns every match as a list of strings.

tasks.description: Use `re.sub()` to replace all vowels in 'Hello World' with '*'. Print the result.
tasks.hint:
`re.sub(pattern, replacement, string)` replaces all matches with the replacement.
Pattern for vowels: `r'[aeiouAEIOU]'` — `[...]` is a character class.
`re.sub(r'[aeiouAEIOU]', '*', 'Hello World')` → `'H*ll* W*rld'`
tasks.walkthrough:
The square brackets make a character class: any single vowel, either case.
`sub` replaces each match with `*`.

tasks.description: Validate that a string looks like an email address using `re.match()`. Test with 'user@example.com' and 'notanemail'.
tasks.hint:
Simple email pattern: `r'^[\w.+-]+@[\w-]+\.[a-zA-Z]{2,}$'`
`re.match()` checks from the START of the string.
Print True/False for each test case — real email validation is complex, this is a simplified version.
tasks.solution:
import re

pattern = r'^[\w.+-]+@[\w-]+\.[a-zA-Z]{2,}$'

for email in ['user@example.com', 'notanemail']:
    print(bool(re.match(pattern, email)))
tasks.walkthrough:
Reading the pattern left to right: start of string, one or more name characters, an @, one or more domain characters, a literal dot, at least two letters, end of string.
`match` anchors at the start and the `$` anchors at the end, so the whole string must fit.

tasks.description: Use `re.split()` to split the string 'one1two2three3four' on any digit. Print the resulting list.
tasks.hint:
`re.split(pattern, string)` splits wherever the pattern matches.
Pattern `r'\d'` matches any single digit.
`re.split(r'\d', 'one1two2three3four')` → `['one', 'two', 'three', 'four']`
tasks.walkthrough:
`split` cuts the string at every place the pattern matches. Each single digit is a cut point.
The digits themselves are not included in the result.

lesson.intro:
Regular expressions are patterns for matching text: "one or more digits",
"something that looks like an email". They're a small language of their own,
cryptic at first, and enormously useful once a few pieces make sense. Today
covers the handful you'll actually use.

sections.heading: search: is the pattern in there?
sections.body:
`re.search(pattern, text)` returns a match object if the pattern appears
anywhere, or `None` if not. Wrapping it in `bool()` gives a clean True/False.
Patterns are usually written as raw strings, `r'...'`, so backslashes are
left alone.
sections.code:
import re

print(bool(re.search('World', 'Hello, World!')))
print(bool(re.search('Mars', 'Hello, World!')))

sections.heading: The building blocks
sections.body:
- `\d` any digit, `\w` any letter/digit/underscore, `\s` any whitespace, `.` anything.
- `+` one or more of the previous thing, `*` zero or more, `?` optional.
- `[aeiou]` any one character from the set. `[a-z]` a range.
- `^` start of the string, `$` end of the string.
- `{2,}` at least two of the previous thing.
sections.code:
import re

text = 'I have 3 cats and 12 dogs'
print(re.findall(r'\d+', text))
print(re.findall(r'[aeiou]', 'hello'))

sections.heading: findall, sub, split
sections.body:
`findall` gives every match as a list. `sub` replaces every match. `split`
cuts the string wherever the pattern matches. The results of `findall` are
strings, even when they look like numbers.

sections.heading: match: from the very start
sections.body:
`re.match` only succeeds if the pattern matches at the beginning. Combined
with `$` at the end, it checks the whole string. This is a simplified email
pattern; real validation is messier, but this catches the obvious.
sections.code:
import re

pattern = r'^[\w.+-]+@[\w-]+\.[a-zA-Z]{2,}$'
for s in ['user@example.com', 'notanemail']:
    print(s, bool(re.match(pattern, s)))

watch_out: Forgetting the `r` prefix. `'\d'` in a normal string can be mangled; `r'\d'` is safe.
`re.match` only checks the start. Use `re.search` to find a pattern anywhere.
`findall` returns strings. Convert with `int()` if you need numbers.
`.` matches any character. To match a literal dot, escape it: `\.`.
